headline: Jeffrey's in 210 feet: haddock stacked on the mud, cod tucked to the gravel edge
subhead: A stable week out of Rye put solid groundfish in the box while the first real tuna sign showed up on the ledge's northeast corner.
body_markdown:
Two-ten feet of soft green mud on the northeast flat of Jeffrey's, that's where I spent most of Tuesday, and it held haddock the way it's supposed to this time of year — not a blitz, but a steady pick, fish in the 3 to 5 pound range coming over the rail two and three at a time on diamond jigs tipped with clam. When the mud produces like that in early August, it usually means the water column above it hasn't scattered the bait yet, and that's exactly what we're seeing — sand eels holding tight, mackerel schools working the upper thirty feet, and the haddock parked right underneath where they don't have to work for a meal.

Cod is a different conversation, and it's a gravel conversation. I moved off the mud basin and ran west to the harder bottom in about 150 feet, the rocky transition zone where the ledge kicks up before it drops back into Scantum Basin. That gravel edge has been the more consistent cod producer than the deeper structure lately — fish in the 8 to 15 pound class, a few pushing 20, taking jigging spoons worked with a short hop off bottom, and skate-baited hooks on a high-low rig for the guys who'd rather sit still. The key this week has been staying tight to the break itself. Drift fifty yards off it onto flat mud and the cod disappear; hold the edge and they're there. That's been true on both the outgoing and incoming tide, though the bite windows have run a little longer on the ebb, probably because the current's pushing bait right along that gravel lip instead of lifting it off.

Platts Bank was quieter than I'd like this week. I checked it Thursday in about 195 feet and came away with pollock instead of the cod I was hoping for — decent fish, 6 to 10 pounds, hitting diamond jigs on the drop, but the cod bite there has been spotty enough that I'm not sending anyone out of their way for it right now. Tillies Bank I haven't fished since last week, and I'd rather tell you that plainly than guess at it. If you're running that far, call around the harbor first.

Now for the tuna, because this is the part of the report that's actually building the way I thought it would. We flagged last week that the bait holding on the ledge would drag the bluefin pattern along gradually through August, and that's what's happening — not a giant show yet, that's an October conversation off Jeffrey's, but school-class and mid-size bluefin have started working the approaches to Stellwagen and the southern stretch of the ledge where the mackerel schools have been thickest. I had two boats radio in feed sightings Wednesday afternoon, birds working hard over breaking bait about three miles off Thatcher Island, and one of them stuck a fish in the 150-pound class trolling a spreader bar through the melee. It's early, it's scattered, and you need to be willing to run and gun rather than anchor up and wait, but the ingredients are there. Mackerel jigged fresh off the rail and either live-lined or chunked out the back has been the better play than trolling alone when you find working birds — the fish seem to want something natural in the slick, not just something moving fast past them.

Conditions have cooperated. We've had a stretch of light southwest wind and settled seas out of Rye, the kind of stable high-pressure window that lets you actually work the ledge methodically instead of getting bounced off it by afternoon chop. That stability is part of why the tuna sign has been building steadily rather than showing up in one big push — the bait's had time to set up and hold instead of getting scattered by wind-driven seas. Tide's been unremarkable, nothing extreme either way, which for groundfish purposes just means the bite windows have been tied more to time of day than tide stage — early morning and the last two hours of daylight have both produced better than midday on both the gravel and the mud.

Looking ahead, if this weather pattern holds through the weekend I'd keep working the same two zones — mud basin for haddock, gravel edge for cod — and I'd make at least one pass toward the Stellwagen approaches with jigs rigged and ready in case you run into working birds. The tuna pattern should keep building through the rest of August as long as the mackerel stay put, but it's still a find-the-feed operation right now, not a set-your-anchor one. If the wind swings onshore and kicks up the kind of chop that scatters bait off the surface, I'd expect the tuna sign to go quiet fast and I'd shift the whole day back to bottom fishing on the ledge, where the fish don't care what the wind's doing forty feet above their heads.
